title: Hiralal And Ors4. And V.Raja Kumari vs . P.Subbarama Naidu And Anr.5]. It on 29 August, 2012
full_text: Hiralal And Ors4. And V.Raja Kumari vs . P.Subbarama Naidu And Anr.5]. It on 29 August, 2012 In the Court of Sh. Manoj Kumar : Senior Civil Judge­cum­Metropolitan Magistrate of New Delhi District at Patiala House Courts, New Delhi C.C. No. 915/1/09 Unique ID No. 02403R0605772006 In the matter of: Smt. Shakuntla Sharma, Wife of Shri Satyavir Sharma, R/o C­31, B. K. Dutt Colony, New Delhi­110003. ....................Complainant VERSUS Smt. Savita Singhal, Wife of Shri Pankaj Singhal, R/o F­52, Khanpur Extn., New Delhi. .......................Accused Date of Institution : 17.11.2006 Date of Arguments: 16.8.2012 Date of Judgment : 29.8.2012 COMPLAINT UNDER SECTION 138 OF THE NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS ACT, 1881. JUDGMENT : The present case was received by way of transfer as per the order no. 145­192/01/F.3(4)/MM dated 02.01.2009 passed by the learned District Judge­I and Sessions Judge, Delhi in pursuance of order no. C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 1 of 26 25/DHC/Gaz./VI.E2(a) dated 22.10.2008 passed by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court. It shall be disposed of in compliance of the said orders. 2. This is a complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Act 26 of 1881) made by complainant Smt. Shakuntla Sharma against accused Smt. Savita Singhal stating that in the first week of January, 2004 the accused had borrowed Rs.2,25,000/­, as friendly loan, from the complainant; that thereafter, after a great persuasion, to discharge her debt the accused had issued two cheques bearing nos. 316969 and 422124 both dated 25.8.2006 in the sum of Rs.2,00,000/­ and Rs.25,000/­ respectively drawn on Syndicate Bank, Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, D.T.C. Depot, Khanpur, New Delhi branch in favour of the complainant; that on two occasions the complainant had presented the said two cheques for encashment through her banker the State Bank of India, South Extension, Part­II, New Delhi branch but on both the occasions the same returned unpaid alongwith memos dated 29.8.2006 and 09.9.2006 with remarks "Funds Insufficient and Account Freeze"; that the complainant had informed the accused about the dishonour of the said two cheques and requested to pay the cheque amount, but the accused flatly refused to pay the cheque amount to the complainant; that the complainant, through her counsel, had sent a legal notice dated 05.10.2006 to the accused by registered AD and UPC demanding the cheque amount but the accused neither replied the same nor paid the cheque amount leading up to the C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 2 of 26 making of the present complaint with a view to prosecute and punish the accused for having committed offence punishable under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881. 3. The complaint was made on 17.11.2006 and on 03.5.2007 the complainant was examined under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ( Cr.P.C .) by way of her affidavit. Alongwith her affidavit the complainant also tendered some documents on the basis of which the order under section 204 of Cr.P.C. was passed whereby the accused was summoned to face accusation under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 in respect of cheques no. 316969 and 422124. 4. In pursuance of the process issued by the court the accused appeared before the court and was admitted to bail. Subsequently, on 02.02.2009 a notice of accusation under section 251 Cr.P.C. was framed against the accused whereby she was charged with the commission of offence punishable under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 in respect of cheques no. 316969 and 422124. The notice of accusation was read over and explained to the accused to which she did not plead guilty. 5. In support of her case the complainant got examined herself as CW1 and during her examination in chief tendered her affidavit Ex. CW1/A alongwith documents Ex. CW1/1 to Ex. CW1/7. The witness was cross examined on behalf of the accused and subsequently evidence on behalf of the complainant was closed on 27.5.2011. On 14.10.2011 the accused was C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 3 of 26 examined under section 313 Cr.P.C. 6. During her examination under section 313 Cr.P.C. the accused denied having taken any loan from the complainant. The accused also denied having drawn cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 in favour of the complainant. The accused further stated that cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 did not belong to her and the same were never drawn by her in favour of the complainant. The accused further stated that in the year 2004 the police had raided her house and she was sent to jail. The accused further stated that her bank account at Khanpur was frozen by the police. The accused denied having received any notice dated 05.10.2006; and stated that the address on notice Ex. CW1/5 did not pertain to her. 7. In her defence the accused got examined DW1 Mr. P.C. Singla, Branch Manager, Syndicate Bank, Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, D.T.C. Depot, Khanpur, New Delhi. 8. I have heard counsel for the parties and gone through the material on record carefully. 9. Having drawn my attention on the testimonies of CW1 Smt. Shakuntla Sharma, DW1 Mr. P.C. Singla and documents Ex. CW1/1 to Ex. CW1/7 and the law laid down in Subodh S. Salaskar v. Jayprakash M. Shah & another , AIR 2008 SC 3086 and Jain Associates and others v. Deepak Chawdhary , 1999 [2] JCC [Delhi] 383 it is submitted by counsel for the complainant that having taken friendly loan of Rs.2,25,000/­ from the C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 4 of 26 complainant to discharge her debt liability the accused had drawn cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 both dated 25.8.2006 in the sum of Rs. 2,00,000/­ and Rs.25,000/­ respectively in favour of the complainant on her account maintained at the Syndicate Bank, Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, DTC Depot, Khanpur, New Delhi branch and when the said cheques were presented by the complainant for encashment, the same returned unpaid alongwith memos Ex. CW1/3 and Ex. CW1/4 both dated 09.9.2006 due to insufficient funds in the account of the accused and account being frozen. It is further submitted by counsel for the complainant that after return of cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 as dishonoured a legal notice dated 05.10.2006, a copy of which is Ex. CW1/5, was sent by the complainant to the accused on 06.10.2006 by registered post with AD and UPC vide receipts Ex. CW1/6 and Ex. CW1/7 whereby the accused was called upon to make payment of the cheque amount within fifteen days of the receipt of the notice which was sent at the correct address of the accused but despite receipt of the notice the accused did not make payment of cheque amount within fifteen days. It is further submitted by counsel for the complainant that all the ingredients of offence punishable under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 and the conditions precedent for making the complaint have been proved in this case and therefore, the accused be convicted and punished for having committed offence committed under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 in respect of cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2. It is also submitted by C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 5 of 26 counsel for the complainant that the defence taken by the accused is frivolous and corrections in notice dated 05.10.2006 were made before dispatching the same at the correct address of the accused. 10. Per­contra, having drawn my attention on the testimony of CW1 Smt. Shakuntla Sharma, DW1 Mr. P.C. Singla, cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2, memoranda Ex. CW1/3 and Ex. CW1/4, copy of notice Ex. CW1/5 and copy of receipts Ex. CW1/6 and Ex. CW1/7, certified copies of the orders Ex. CW1/DA and Ex. CW1/DB, certificate Ex. DW1/A, statement of account Ex. DW1/B and the law laid down in HDFC Bank Limited v. Amit Kumar Singh , 160 ( 2009) Delhi Law Times 478, Sridhar M.A. v. Metalloy N. Steel Corporation , (2000) 1 Supreme Court Cases 397, Jugesh Sehgal v. Shamsher Singh Gogi , (2009) 14 Supreme Court Cases 683, K. Annaji Rao v. N. Krishna Raj Shekhar and another, 2004 Cri. L. J. 2911, Standard Chartered Bank & another v. State & another, 52 (2008) Delhi Law Times 65, Vijay Chaudhary v. Gyan Chand Jain, 2008 [3] JCC [NI] 297, Onkar Nath Goenka v. M/s Gujarat Lease Finance Ltd., 2009 [2] JCC [NI] 109 it is submitted by counsel for the accused that the complainant has failed to prove all the ingredients of offence punishable under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 and the conditions precedent for making the complaint in respect of cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 and therefore, the accused is entitled to be acquitted. It is further submitted by counsel for the accused that cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 were never drawn by C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 6 of 26 the accused in favour of the complainant to discharge any legally enforceable debt or liability and instead during a police raid in the year 2004 at the house of the accused the cheque books containing leaves number 316969 and 422124 were misplaced which have been misused by the complainant. It is also submitted by counsel for the accused that no notice was ever sent by the complainant to the accused before making of the present complaint and therefore, the condition laid down in clause (b) of proviso to section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 has not been met and consequently, no offence can be attributed to the accused in respect of cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2. It is also submitted by counsel for the accused that as per memos Ex. CW1/3 and Ex. CW1/4 the cheques in question returned unpaid as the account was frozen and therefore, the dishonour of the cheques does not fall within the ambit of section 138 of Act 26 of 1881. 11. I have given my thoughtful consideration to the submission made on behalf of the parties. 12. Section 138 of the Act 26 of 1881 which pertains to dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account reads as follows: 138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account ― Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 7 of 26 made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless­ (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation­ For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. 13. From a reading of section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 it can be discerned that to hold a person liable for the commission of the offence created by the said section it is necessary to prove that the cheque in question was issued by the accused and the same was presented by the complainant for encashment and upon such presentation the cheque returned unpaid by the banker of the accused due to insufficient funds in the account of the accused or due to exceeding arrangement. It is also necessary to prove that after return of the cheque in question a notice in terms of the proviso to the said section was served on the person sought to be made liable; and despite service of notice, neither any payment was C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 8 of 26 made nor other obligations, if any, were complied within fifteen days from the date of the receipt of the notice. From a reading of section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 it also becomes indisputable that unless the conditions precedent as mentioned in the proviso to section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 are satisfied the accused cannot be held guilty. 14. In Raj Kumar Khurana v. State of (NCT of Delhi) and Anr. , 2009 AIR SCW 3966 having held that the provisions of section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 must be interpreted strictly the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed as follows: 10. A bare perusal of the aforementioned provision would clearly go to show that by reason thereof a legal fiction has been created. A legal fiction, as is well known, although is required to be given full effect, has its own limitations. It cannot be taken recourse to for any purpose other than the one mentioned in the statute itself. In State of A.P. and Anr. v. A.P. Pensioners Association and Ors. [(2005) 13 SCC 161], this Court held : "...In other words, all the consequences ordinarily flowing from a rule would be given effect to if the rule otherwise does not limit the operation thereof. If the rule itself provides a limitation on its operation, the consequences flowing from the legal fiction have to be understood in the light of the limitations prescribed. Thus, it is not possible to construe the legal fiction as simply as suggested by Mr. Lalit." 11. Section 138 of the Act moreover provides for a penal provision. A penal provision created by reason of a legal fiction must receive strict construction. [See R. Kalyani v. Janak C. Mehta and Ors. ( 2009) 1 SCC 516 and DCM Financial Services Ltd. v. J.N. Sareen and Anr. (2008) 8 SCC 1]. Such a penal provision, enacted in terms of the legal fiction drawn would be attracted when a cheque is returned by the bank unpaid. Such non­payment may either be : (i) because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque, or (ii) it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank. C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 9 of 26 Before a proceeding thereunder is initiated, all the legal requirements therefor must be complied with. The court must be satisfied that all the ingredients of commission of an offence under the said provision have been complied with. The parameters for invoking the provisions of Section 138 of the Act, thus, being limited, we are of the opinion that refusal on the part of the bank to honour the cheque would not bring the matter within the mischief of the provisions of Section 138 of the Act. 15. In the present case before analysing the evidence and appreciating the arguments advanced on behalf of the parties the general condition of the documents Ex. CW1/1, Ex. CW1/2, Ex. CW1/3, Ex. CW1/4, Ex. CW1/5, Ex. CW1/6 and Ex. CW1/7 is required to be discussed. As per the contents of cheque Ex. CW1/1 the same is bearing number 316969 and dated 25.8.2006. The cheque has been drawn on account no. 6226 maintained by accused Savita Singhal at Syndicate Bank, Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, DTC Depot, Khanpur, New Delhi branch and the sum indicated therein, in words and figures, is Rs.2,00,000/­. The date in cheque Ex. CW1/1 is in black ink. The name of the payee in cheque Ex. CW1/1 is in dark blue colour. The amount in words and figures in Ex. CW1/1 is in light blue colour and the same has been signed in black ink. At the reverse of cheque Ex. CW1/1 it has been written, inter alia, "A/c Freezed as per FIR No. 14/2004 12.1.04 us 420/406/120B/34 IPC ." 16. As per the contents of cheque Ex. CW1/2 the same is bearing number 422124 and dated 25.8.2006. The cheque has been drawn on C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 10 of 26 account no. 6226 maintained by accused Savita Singhal at Syndicate Bank, Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, DTC Depot, Khanpur, New Delhi branch and the sum indicated therein, in words and figures, is Rs.25,000/­. The date in cheque Ex. CW1/2 is in dark blue ink. The name of the payee in cheque Ex. CW1/2 is also in dark blue ink, but apparently, in different handwriting. The amount in words and figures in Ex. CW1/2 is in light blue greenish ink and the same has been signed in light blue greenish ink similar to the ink used in writing the amount in words and figures. 17. As per the contents of memos Ex. CW1/3 and Ex. CW1/4 the same were issued by Syndicate Bank, Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, DTC Depot, Khanpur, New Delhi branch on 09.9.2006 and indicate that on presentation for encashment cheques bearing numbers 422124 and 316969 returned unpaid due to insufficient funds and the reason "A/c Freezed". 18. As per the contents of Ex. CW1/5, which purports to be a copy of notice dated 05.10.2006 sent by the complainant through her counsel Mrs. Debakie Rani Sharma to the accused, initially the name and address of the addressee was mentioned as Smt. Savita Singhal, w/o Shri Pankaj Singhal, r/o 52, Khanpur, New Delhi, which was subsequently corrected to Smt. Savita Singhal, w/o Shri Pankaj Singhal, r/o F­52, Khanpur, Extn., New Delhi­62. The office copy Ex. CW1/5 has been signed by Smt. Debakie Rani Sharma, Advocate. 19. As per the contents of Ex. CW1/6, comprising of two postal C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 11 of 26 receipts bearing numbers 5455 and 5456, two postal articles under registered cover were addressed to Shri Pankaj Singhal, New Delhi and Smt. Savita Singhal, New Delhi respectively on 06.10.2006. In both the receipts besides the name of the addressee and the name of their city, no other particulars have been mentioned. 20. On Ex. CW1/7, which purports to be a UPC receipt, names and addresses of two persons namely, Smt. Savita Singhal, w/o Shri Pankaj Singhal, r/o F­52, Khanpur Extn., New Delhi­62 and Shri Pankaj Singhal, r/o F­52, Khanpur Extn., New Delhi­62 have been mentioned. The receipt is a joint receipt whereupon one postal stamp of Rs.3/­ denomination has been affixed. 21. In the present case from the testimony of CW1 Smt. Shakuntla Sharma and the statement of accused made under section 313 of Cr.P.C. it has been proved that cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 are bearing signatures of accused Savita Singhal. As per the version of the complainant both the cheques were handed over by the husband of the accused to her on 25.8.2006 at her residence whereas as per the version of the accused, as taken during her examination under section 313 of Cr.P.C., the cheques were never drawn by her in favour of the complainant to discharge any debt and instead during a raid by the police at her residence in the year 2004, the cheque book containing both the cheques, which were lying in the respective cheque books were misplaced. Curiously, during the course of C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 12 of 26 arguments counsel for the accused having done volte face submitted that the complainant has lied before this court by stating that the cheques were received by her on 25.8.2006 instead the same were received by her in the year 2002. As the accused has failed to bring to the notice of the court any plausible evidence to suggest that the cheques came in possession of the complainant after their misplacement during the police raid in the year 2004, therefore, the court does not believe the version of the accused that both the cheques were not delivered by her or on her behalf to the complainant. 22. From the testimonies of CW1 Smt. Shakuntla Sharma, DW1 Mr. P.C. Singla, Senior Branch Manager, Syndicate Bank, Khanpur, New Delhi and documents Ex. CW1/1, Ex. CW1/2, Ex. CW1/3 and Ex. CW1/4 it has also been proved that cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 were presented by the complainant for encashment and upon such presentation the same returned unpaid for the reasons "Funds Insufficient" and "A/c Freezed". 23. It is submitted by counsel for the accused that since the account of the accused was freezed as per the order of the police and the accused was not in a position to do any transaction through her banker, therefore, no liability under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 can be fastened upon the accused. On the other hand at the strength of documents Ex. CW1/3 and Ex. CW1/4 and the testimony of DW1 Mr. P.C. Singla it is C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 13 of 26 argued on behalf of the complainant that the accused has failed to prove that the account of the accused whereupon cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 were drawn was freezed by the order of any police officer or court; and that from the testimony of DW1 Mr. P. C. Singla it has been proved that the account could have been freezed for being dormant due to the act of the accused herself. It is also argued on behalf of the complainant that the cheques in question returned unpaid not only for the reason "A/c Freezed" but also for "Insufficient Funds" and therefore, the accused is liable. 24. No doubt, during his examination DW1 Mr. P. C. Singla has opined that an account may be freezed on account of becoming dormant account when no transaction took place over a period of time but he had also stated that the account can be freezed as per the instructions of a police officer, court or other authority. Nevertheless, in the face of the endorsement put by the banker of the accused on the reverse of cheque Ex. CW1/1, while both the cheques remained in the custody of the complainant, there remains no doubt that as on 09.9.2006, the account of the accused against which cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2 were drawn was freezed in connection with a police case bearing FIR No. 14/2004, under sections 420 / 406 / 120B / 34 IPC. Further, as per the statement of account Ex. DW1/A during the period 2001 and 2006 the account no.6226 in the name of the accused remained operative and the same was not dormant. 25. In Vijay Chaudhary's case (supra) the account of the drawer of C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 14 of 26 the cheque was attached during the period between issuance of the cheque and its presentation for collection of the amount of the cheque and consequently the cheque presented by the payee for encashment returned unpaid. In the facts of the case the Hon'ble Delhi High Court held that since the account was attached not by the act of the drawer, therefore, no liability under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 could be fastened on the accused. 26. Further in Onkar Nath Goenka's case (supra) the drawer of the cheque by virtue of the order of the DRT of Delhi and the order of CBI by virtue of which his account was freezed, was debarred from complying with the legal notice which led to the dishonour of the cheques. It was held by the Hon'ble High Court that since the account was freezed therefore, no offence punishable under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 was made against the drawer of the cheque and quashed the complaint filed against him. 27. In the present case a perusal of the evidence led by the complainant reveals that both the cheques were presented for encashment on two occasions. First time both the cheque returned unpaid on 29.8.2006 only due to the reason "Insufficient Funds". On the basis of the dishonour of the cheques on 29.8.2006 no legal notice was issued and instead the complainant had chosen to present the cheques again for encashment and in fact as appears from memoranda dated 09.9.2006, both the cheques were again presented for encashment and returned unpaid for the reasons "Insufficient funds" as well as "A/c Freezed". From the perusal of C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 15 of 26 documents Ex. CW1/3 and Ex. CW1/4 it is obvious that prior to 29.8.2006 the account of the accused was not freezed, and it appears that the account was freezed only during the period 29.8.2006 and 09.9.2006. If so was the case then in the face of the freezing of account by the police, it was impossible for the accused to do any transaction through her bank account including maintaining amount to honour cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2. In these circumstances the return of the cheques as unpaid due to the reason "Insufficient Funds" in the account of the accused become inconsequential. 28. In the light of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Vijay Chaudhary's case (supra) and Onkar Nath Goenka's case (supra) I hold that since the account of the accused was freezed and consequently she had lost control over the operation of such bank account, therefore, no liability under section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 can be fastened upon her in respect of cheques Ex. CW1/1 and Ex. CW1/2. 29. It has been deposed by CW1 Smt. Shakuntla Sharma that after return of the cheques as dishonoured a demand notice dated 05.10.2006 was sent by her through her counsel to the accused on 06.10.2006 whereby the accused was called upon to make payment against both the cheques but despite receipt of the notice the accused did not make payment. On the other hand the stand of the accused is that she has never received any notice dated 05.10.2006, a copy of which is Ex. CW1/5. According to the accused C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 16 of 26 no notice was sent on her correct address and therefore, there was no question of receipt of the notice. 30. Having drawn my attention on the law laid down in Subodh S. Salaskar 's case ( supra) and Jain Associates 's case (supra) it is contended by counsel for the complainant that notice was properly addressed to the accused and the same was received. It is further submitted by counsel for the complainant that even if the notice was not received by the accused still in the light of the judgment passed by Hon'ble Supreme Court in C. C. Alvi Haji v. Palapetty Mohd. and another , (2007) 6 SCC 555 the accused must have made payment against the cheques within fifteen days of the receipt of the summons of this court; and since the accused has failed to do so, therefore, she cannot take the defence that notice was never received by her. On the other hand it is argued on behalf of counsel for the accused that the ratio of the decision of the Supreme Court in C. C. Alvi Haji 's case (supra) and consequently Subodh S. Salaskar 's case (supra) is applicable only in a case where initial presumptions under section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (Act 10 of 1897) and section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (Act 1 of 1872) are raised in favour of a party and other party disputes such presumptions. It is also submitted by counsel for the accused that in the present case as the complainant has failed to prove that the notice in question was sent at correct address of the accused, therefore, no presumptions under section 27 of Act 10 of 1897 and section 114 of Act 1 of C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 17 of 26 1872 can be raised against the accused. 31. In Subodh S. Salaskar 's case (supra) having discussed the provisions of section 27 of Act 10 of 1897 and section 114 of Act 1 of 1872 it has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court as under:­ 21. In terms of the provisions of the General Clauses Act , a notice must be deemed to have been served in the ordinary course subject to the fulfillment of the conditions laid down therein. Section 27 of the General Clauses Act reads as under : "27. Meaning of service by post. ­ Where any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this. Act authorises or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression 'serve' or either of the expression 'give' or 'send' or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, pre­paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post." Thirty days' time ordinarily must be held to be sufficient for service of notice. In fact when the service of notice is sought to be effected by Speed Post, ordinarily the service takes place within a few days. Even under Order V, Rule 9(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure , 1908, summons is presumed to be served if it does not come back within thirty days. In a situation of this nature, there was no occasion for the Court to hold that service of notice could not be effected within a period of thirty days. 22. Presumption of service, under the statute, would arise not only when it is sent by registered post in terms of Section 27 of the General Clauses Act but such a presumption may be raised also under Section 114 of the Evidence Act. Even when a notice is received back with an endorsement that the party has refused to accept, still then a presumption can be raised as regards the valid service of notice. Such a notice, as has been held by a Three­Judge Bench of this Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed and Another [(2007) 6 SCC 555] should be construed liberally, stating : "17. It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of criminal law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 18 of 26 notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the GC Act and Section 114 of the Evidence. Act. In our view, any­other interpretation of the proviso would defeat the very object of the legislation. As observed in Bhaskaran case if the "giving ofnotice" in the context of Clause(b) of the proviso was the same as the "receipt of notice" a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by adopting different strategies and escape from legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act." 32. Further in C. C. Alvi Haji 's case (supra) the Hon'ble Supreme Court having discussed the provisions of section 27 of Act 10 of 1897 and section 114 of Act 1 of 1872 held as follows:­ 10. It is, thus, trite to say that where the payee dispatches the notice by registered post with correct address of the drawer of the cheque, the principle incorporated in Section 27 of the G.C. Act would be attracted; the requirement of Clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of the Act stands complied with and cause of action to file a complaint arises on the expiry of the period prescribed in Clause (c) of the said proviso for payment by the drawer of the cheque. Nevertheless, it would be without prejudice to the right of the drawer to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address. 11. However, the Referring Bench was of the view that this Court in Vinod Shivappas case (supra) did not take note of Section 114 of Evidence Act in its proper perspective. It felt that the presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act being a rebuttable presumption, the complaint should contain necessary averments to raise the presumption of service of notice; that it was not sufficient for a complainant to state that a notice was sent by registered C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 19 of 26 post and that the notice was returned with the endorsement "out of station"; and that there should be a further averment that the addressee­drawer had deliberately avoided receiving the notice or that the addressee had knowledge of the notice, for raising a presumption under Section 114 of Evidence Act. 12. Therefore, the moot question requiring consideration is in regard to the implication of Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 insofar as the service of notice under the said proviso is concerned. Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 reads as follows : " Section 114 ­ Court may presume existence of certain facts.­ The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened. Regard being had to the common course of natural events human conduct and public and private business, in their relation to the facts of the particular case. Illustrations The Court may presume­ ..... ...... ...... (f) That the common course of business has been followed in particular cases; ....... ........ ...." 13. According to Section 114 of the Act, read with illustration (f) thereunder, when it appears to the Court that the common course of business renders it probable that a thing would happen, the Court may draw presumption that the thing would have happened, unless there are circumstances in a particular case to show that the common course of business was not followed. Thus, Section 114 enables the Court to presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business in their relation to the facts of the particular case. Consequently, the court can presume that the common course of business has been followed in particular cases. When applied to communications sent by post, Section 114 enables the Court to presume that in the common course of natural events, the communication would have been delivered at the address of the addressee. But the presumption that is raised under Section 27 of the G.C. Act is a far stronger presumption. Further, while Section 114 of Evidence Act refers to a general presumption, Section 27 refers to a specific presumption. For the sake of ready reference. Section 27 of G.C. Act is extracted below : "27. Meaning of service by post.­ Where any Central Act or Regulation C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 20 of 26 made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression "serve" or either of the expressions "give" or "send" or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, pre­paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post." 14. Section 27 gives rise to a presumption that service of notice has been effected when it is sent to the correct address by registered post. In view of the said presumption, when stating that a notice has been sent by registered post to the address of the drawer, it is unnecessary to further aver in the complaint that in spite of the return of the notice unserved, it is deemed to have been served or that the addressee is deemed to have knowledge of the notice. Unless and until the contrary is proved by the addressee, service of notice is deemed to have been effected at the time at which the letter would have been delivered in the ordinary course of business. This Court has already held that when a notice is sent by registered post and is returned with a postal endorsement "refused" or "not available in the house" or "house locked" or "shop closed" or "addressee not in station," due service has to be presumed. [ Vide Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh3 ; State of M.P. v. Hiralal and Ors4 . and V.Raja Kumari Vs. P.Subbarama Naidu and Anr.5 ]. It is, therefore, manifest that in view of the presumption available under Section 27 of the Act, it is not necessary to aver in the complaint under Section 138 of the Act that service of notice was evaded by the accused or that the accused had a role to play in the return of the notice unserved. 3. AIR 1992 SC 1604 4. (1996) 7 SCC 523 5. (2004) 8 SCC 774 15. Insofar as the question of disclosure of necessary particulars with regard to the issue of notice in terms of proviso (b) of Section 138 of the Act, in order to enable the Court to draw presumption or inference either under Section 27 of the G.C. Act or Section 114 of the Evidence Act, is concerned, there is no material difference between the two provisions. In our opinion, therefore, when the notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing the drawer of the cheque, the mandatory requirement of issue of notice in terms of Clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of the Act stands complied with. It is needless to emphasise that the complaint must contain basic facts regarding the mode and manner of the issuance of notice to the drawer of the C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 21 of 26 cheque. It is well settled that at the time of taking cognizance of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, the Court is required to be prima facie satisfied that a case under the said Section is made out and the aforenoted mandatory statutory procedural requirements have been complied with. It is then for the drawer to rebut the presumption about the service of notice and show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address or that the address mentioned on the cover was incorrect or that the letter was never tendered or that the report of the postman was incorrect. In our opinion, this interpretation of the provision would effectuate the object and purpose for which proviso to Section 138 was enacted, namely, to avoid unnecessary hardship, to an honest drawer of a cheque and to vide him an opportunity to make amends. 16. As noticed above, the entire purpose of requiring a notice is to give an opportunity to the drawer to pay the cheque amount within 15 days of service of notice and thereby free himself from the penal consequences of Section 138. In Vinod Shivappa (supra), this Court observed : "One can also conceive of cases where a well intentioned drawer may have inadvertently missed to make necessary arrangements for reasons beyond his control, even though he genuinely intended to honour the cheque drawn by him. The law treats such lapses induced by inadvertence or negligence to be pardonable, provided the drawer after notice makes amends and pays the amount within the prescribed period. It is for this reason that Clause (c) of proviso to Section 138 provides that the section shall not apply unless the drawer of the cheque fails to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. To repeat, the proviso is meant to protect honest drawers whose cheques may have been dishonoured for the fault of others, or who may have genuinely wanted to fulfil their promise but on account of inadvertence or negligence failed to make necessary arrangements for the payment of the cheque. The proviso is not meant to protect unscrupulous drawers who never intended to honour the cheques issued by them, it being a part of their modus operandi to cheat unsuspecting persons. 17. It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of Criminal Law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the Court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 22 of 26 summons from the Court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the G.C. Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the proviso would defeat the very object of the legislation. As observed in Bhaskaran's case (supra), if the giving of notice in the context of Clause (b) of the proviso was the same as the 'receipt of notice' a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by adopting different strategies and escape from legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act. (Emphasis added). 33. It has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sridhar M.A. v. Mettaloy N. Steel Corporation , (2000) 1 SCC 397 that although in appropriate case deemed service is to be accepted by court, but such presumption of deemed service is not a matter of course in all cases. 34. From a reading of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C. C. Alvi Haji 's case ( supra) and Subodh S. Salaskar 's case (supra) it is obvious that before imposing disability on an accused for his not making payment to the complainant of the cheque amount within fifteen days of the receipt of summons alongwith the complaint, it is sine qua non that the presumptions under section 27 of Act 10 of 1897 and section 114 of Act 1 of 1872 must be operating in favour of such complainant and against the accused. If there is no ground for raising presumptions under section 27 of Act 10 of 1897 and section 114 of Act 1 of 1872 then the accused cannot be precluded from raising his defence on the ground that the requirement of clause (b) of proviso to section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 is not complied by the C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 23 of 26 complainant. 35. The complainant in her complaint has stated and in her affidavit Ex. It is nowhere deposed by CW1 Smt. Shakunatla Sharma that having put the notice in envelope she herself had dispatched the notice to the accused. A perusal of Ex. Debakie Rani Sharma, Advocate having office at House no. H­60, Gali no.7, New Mahavir Nagar, New Delhi. As already pointed out there are corrections in the address of the accused on notice Ex. CW1/5. Notice Ex. CW1/5 is also bearing reference no. 5106 in the record of counsel of the complainant. According to the complainant the original of Ex. CW1/5 was sent to the accused by registered post with AD and UPC. No acknowledgment card has been produced or proved on behalf of the complainant. A perusal of postal receipt Ex. No witness has been produced on behalf of the complainant from the office of counsel of the complainant to prove as to under what circumstances changes were made in the address of the accused on notice Ex. CW1/5. Neither counsel nor any clerk from the office of counsel of the complainant has been produced alongwith record of the letter bearing reference no. 5106 to prove as to under what circumstances the notice was sent and at what address. In the absence of proof of the circumstances in which the corrections were made in notice Ex. CW1/5; and the address of the accused on receipt Ex. CW1/6 and non production of any acknowledgment card received from the accused this court does not believe the version of the complainant that the notice was sent at the correct address of the accused. Furthermore, since as per the receipt Ex. CW1/7 a letter was sent to the accused as well as other person jointly and not to the accused only, it cannot be believed that by way of Ex. CW1/7 notice was sent to the accused. On the basis of receipts Ex. CW1/6 and Ex. CW1/7 no presumptions can be raised against the accused under section 27 of Act 10 of 1897 and section 114 of Act 1 of 1872. In the face of the defence taken by the accused that she had not received any notice and in the absence of proof of sending of such notice by the complainant by calling her lawyer C. C. No. 915/1/09 Page 25 of 26 who prepared and dispatched the notice or any other person from her office, this court gives benefit of doubt to the accused and holds that it is highly probable that the notice in question dated 05.10.2006 was sent on wrong address of the accused which was subsequently corrected in the office copy and filed in this court. In these circumstances I hold that the complainant has failed to prove the requirement under clause (b) of proviso to section 138 of Act 26 of 1881 that before making the present complaint a legal notice was sent by the complainant to the accused within thirty days of the receipt of the notice and such notice was received by the accused. 37.
